Set the incident report to send an alert after 10 matches across all users

explanation: The instance count on a sensitive information type condition sets how many occurrences must be found in one item for the rule to match, so a minimum of 10 separates high-volume emails from the low-severity rule. Confidence level controls how certain each detection must be, not how many there are. Message size doesn't measure the number of card numbers. Alert aggregation counts matching activities, not numbers within one email.

prompt: An organization wants to detect credit card numbers in Power BI semantic models and notify their owners with policy tips. Which DLP policy location should the administrator select?

options.text: SharePoint sites
Fabric and Power BI
On-premises repositories
Exchange email

explanation: DLP policies can be scoped to the Fabric and Power BI location to detect sensitive information in Power BI semantic models and other supported items. Power BI content isn't evaluated through the SharePoint location. On-premises repositories are scanned by the information protection scanner. The Exchange location evaluates email messages, not Power BI items.

prompt: A company wants to prevent employees from sending U.S. social security numbers in Teams chats and channel messages. Which location should the DLP policy include?

options.text: Exchange email messages
OneDrive accounts of all users
Devices onboarded to Purview
Teams chat and channel messages

explanation: The Teams chat and channel messages location applies DLP to messages in Teams chats and channels. The Exchange location covers email, not Teams messages. OneDrive covers files that users store and share, such as files shared in chats, but not the chat messages. The Devices location applies to activity on onboarded endpoints rather than Teams messages.

prompt: A company has configured Adaptive Protection in insider risk management. It wants an Exchange DLP rule that blocks external sharing of sensitive content only for users whose insider risk level is elevated. Which condition should the rule use?

options.text: Insider risk level for Adaptive Protection is Elevated risk level
Sender is a member of the Insider Risk Management Investigators role group
Content contains the Elevated trainable classifier
Sender's sign-in risk in Microsoft Entra ID Protection is High

explanation: After Adaptive Protection is configured, the Insider risk level for Adaptive Protection is condition becomes available with the values Elevated, Moderate, and Minor, so the rule can target elevated-risk users. Role group membership identifies administrators, not risky users. No trainable classifier represents insider risk levels. Entra ID Protection sign-in risk is a different signal used by Conditional Access, not an insider risk level.

prompt: An administrator creating a DLP policy for Exchange can't find the Insider risk level for Adaptive Protection is condition. What should the administrator do first?

options.text: Add the Devices location to the policy
Set the DLP policy state to Run the policy in simulation mode
Configure Adaptive Protection in Insider Risk Management
Enable optical character recognition for Exchange

explanation: The condition is available only after Adaptive Protection is configured in insider risk management, for example by using quick setup. Adding Devices doesn't make the condition available, and Exchange already supports it. Policy state doesn't control which conditions are offered. OCR extends detection to images and is unrelated to insider risk levels.

prompt: An administrator used quick setup to configure Adaptive Protection. A week later, elevated-risk users are still able to share sensitive content externally by email, although DLP events and alerts are being recorded for them. What is the most likely reason?

options.text: Quick setup creates policies for Devices only
The DLP policies created by quick setup run in simulation mode
Adaptive Protection requires a separate DLP policy for each user
The elevated risk level expires after 24 hours

explanation: Quick setup creates DLP policies, including Adaptive Protection policy for Teams and Exchange DLP, in simulation mode, so they audit and alert but don't block until an administrator turns them on. Quick setup creates policies for Teams and Exchange as well as Devices. Policies target risk levels, not individual users. Risk level expiry wouldn't explain why the policy generates events for these users without blocking.

prompt: An administrator manually creates an Adaptive Protection DLP policy for the Devices location to block elevated-risk users from copying files to USB. The policy doesn't act on users' files. Advanced classification scanning and protection is turned off. What should the administrator do?

options.text: Add the File Type is condition or turn on advanced classification
Add the Exchange location to the same Adaptive Protection policy
Change the insider risk level in the condition to Minor risk level
Assign the policy to the Insider Risk Management role group members

explanation: For Adaptive Protection to work on devices, you must either turn on Advanced classification scanning and protection or, when creating the policy manually, include the File Type is condition. Adding Exchange doesn't affect enforcement on devices. Lowering the risk level would widen who is targeted but not fix enforcement. DLP policies are scoped to users and locations, not to role groups.

prompt: Which three locations support the Insider risk level for Adaptive Protection is condition in DLP policy rules? (Choose three.)

options.text: Exchange Online
SharePoint sites
Devices
Teams
On-premises repositories

explanation: Once Adaptive Protection is configured, the condition is available in rules for policies scoped to Exchange Online, Devices, and Teams. SharePoint sites and on-premises repositories aren't among the locations that support the condition.

prompt: A SharePoint document matches two rules in the same DLP policy. One rule only sends a policy tip, and the other blocks access for people outside the organization. What does DLP enforce on the document?

options.text: Only the policy tip, because it belongs to the rule created first
Both actions, and then the most permissive one
The block action, because the most restrictive action is enforced
Neither action, because conflicting rules cancel each other

explanation: When content matches multiple rules, the first rule evaluated that has the most restrictive action is enforced, so the external block applies; all matches are still recorded in audit logs and reports. Creation order doesn't let a less restrictive rule win. DLP doesn't choose the most permissive action. Conflicting matches don't cancel each other.

prompt: Two endpoint DLP policies apply to the same user and device and both block copying matching files to USB drives. One policy is set to Turn it on and the other is in simulation mode. Which policy's action is applied?

options.text: The policy in simulation mode, because it was created most recently
Neither policy, because a simulation-mode policy disables the other one
Both policies' actions are recorded as audit only, with no block
The policy that is turned on, because enforced policies are preferred

explanation: For endpoints, when actions are identical, policies in Turn it on mode are preferred over policies in simulation mode. Creation date doesn't decide precedence. A simulation-mode policy doesn't disable an enforced policy. The enforced policy blocks the activity rather than just auditing it.

prompt: Two endpoint DLP policies match the same file and both block printing. Policy A lets users override the block, and Policy B doesn't allow an override. What happens when the user tries to print?

options.text: The user can override, because Policy A allows overrides
The print is blocked with no override option
The print is allowed, because the policies conflict
Policy A applies, because it was evaluated first

explanation: For endpoint override options, No override takes precedence over Allow override, so the user is blocked without an override. An override doesn't win against a stricter setting. Conflicting policies don't allow the activity. Evaluation order doesn't let the override setting win over No override.

prompt: An Exchange DLP policy has a higher-priority rule that restricts access by blocking everyone, and a lower-priority rule in another policy that adds an HTML disclaimer. An email matches both rules. What happens?

options.text: The block applies, and the halting action stops further processing
The disclaimer is added first, and then the email is blocked
Only the disclaimer is applied, because it is a non-halting action
Both rules are skipped, because they belong to different policies

explanation: Exchange actions are halting or non-halting; a halting action such as restricting access by blocking everyone stops processing of later rules and policies, so the disclaimer rule isn't processed. Non-halting actions such as adding a disclaimer let processing continue, but here the halting rule runs first. A non-halting action doesn't override a halting one. Rules in different policies are still evaluated in priority order.

prompt: A company uses Box, connected to Microsoft Defender for Cloud Apps. It wants a file policy that detects files containing Microsoft Purview sensitive information types, such as credit card numbers. Which content inspection method should the policy use?

options.text: Built-in regular expressions in the file name filter
Data Classification Services
The MIME type filter
The Sensitivity label filter set to Azure RMS encrypted

explanation: The Data Classification Services inspection method uses Microsoft Purview sensitive information types and is the recommended method for file policies. A file name filter only matches names, not content. The MIME type filter checks file type. The Azure RMS encrypted filter identifies files whose content couldn't be inspected because they're encrypted.

prompt: A Defender for Cloud Apps file policy inspects content for U.S. social security numbers. The security team wants a match only when a file contains at least 20 social security numbers. What should the administrator configure?

options.text: A daily alert limit of 20 for the policy
The policy severity set to High
The minimum number of content violations set to 20
The Apply to setting limited to 20 selected folders

explanation: File policies let you set the minimum number of content violations a file must have before it is considered a violation. The daily alert limit caps the number of alerts per day and doesn't change what counts as a match. Policy severity only affects notifications and prioritization. The Apply to setting controls which folders are scanned, not how many matches are needed.

prompt: A company wants a Defender for Cloud Apps file policy to inspect only files in two specific OneDrive and SharePoint parent folders and their subfolders. How should the policy be scoped?

options.text: Use the Parent folder filter with the Equals operator
Use the Owner OU filter
Use the Access level filter set to Internal for those folders
Set Apply to to Selected folders and add both parent folders

explanation: To act on files in specific parent folders and their subfolders, set Apply to to Selected folders and add each parent folder. The Parent folder filter with Equals applies only to that folder and excludes subfolders. Owner OU applies only to Google Drive files and filters by the owner's organizational unit. Access level filters by sharing level, not location.

prompt: Two Defender for Cloud Apps file policies match the same SharePoint file, and each policy applies a different sensitivity label as its governance action. What should the administrator expect?

options.text: Only the first triggered policy's action is guaranteed to apply
Both labels are applied to the file
The file receives the label with the higher priority
Neither label is applied until an administrator resolves the conflict

explanation: Only the governance action of the first triggered file policy is guaranteed to be applied; a second policy can't apply another sensitivity label to the same file. A file can have only one sensitivity label, so both can't apply. The documented behavior is based on which policy triggers first, not on label priority. The policies don't wait for an administrator to resolve conflicts.

prompt: A company has onboarded its Windows 11 devices to Endpoint DLP. A policy blocks uploading files that contain credit card numbers to unapproved cloud services. Testing shows the block works in Microsoft Edge, but users who upload the same files from Google Chrome are not stopped. What should the administrator do?

options.text: Add chrome.exe to the Unallowed Bluetooth apps list
Deploy the Microsoft Purview extension to Chrome on the devices
Turn on Advanced classification scanning and protection
Add chrome.exe to a removable USB device group

explanation: Service domain upload restrictions apply only in Microsoft Edge or in Chrome and Firefox instances that have the Microsoft Purview extension installed, so deploying the extension closes the gap. The Unallowed Bluetooth apps list controls copying through Bluetooth apps, not browser uploads. Advanced classification improves content detection but does not give DLP visibility into Chrome uploads. Removable USB device groups define storage devices, not applications.

prompt: An organization has already onboarded all of its Windows 10 and Windows 11 devices to Microsoft Defender for Endpoint. The security team now wants to use Endpoint DLP on those devices with the least administrative effort. What should the administrator do?

options.text: Turn on device monitoring in the Microsoft Purview portal
Download and run the Purview onboarding package on each device by using Group Policy
Offboard the devices from Defender for Endpoint and onboard them again by using Intune
Install the Microsoft Purview Information Protection client on each device

explanation: Devices onboarded to Microsoft Defender for Endpoint appear automatically in the Purview device list, so the administrator only needs to turn on device monitoring. Deploying a separate onboarding package by Group Policy or re-onboarding through Intune duplicates work that is already done. The Information Protection client is used for labeling files, not for Endpoint DLP onboarding.

prompt: An administrator onboards several Windows Server 2022 file servers to Microsoft Purview and adds them to the scope of an Endpoint DLP policy. No Endpoint DLP events from the servers appear in Activity explorer. What should the administrator do first?

options.text: Install the Microsoft Purview extension for Microsoft Edge on the servers
Enable Network share coverage and exclusions
Add the servers to a network share group
Turn on Endpoint DLP support for onboarded servers in the Endpoint DLP settings

explanation: Endpoint DLP is not enabled for Windows servers when they are first onboarded; the administrator must turn on Endpoint DLP support for onboarded servers before server events appear in Activity explorer. A browser extension is not needed for Edge and does not enable server monitoring. Network share coverage extends policies to shares that devices connect to, and network share groups define share paths for policy actions; neither enables DLP on the servers themselves.

prompt: An organization plans to use Endpoint DLP on all of its Windows Server computers. Which server configuration is NOT supported by Endpoint DLP?

options.text: Windows Server 2019 Datacenter running as a file server
Windows Server 2022 running as an Azure Virtual Desktop session host
Windows Server 2022 with the Desktop Experience installed
Windows Server 2022 configured as a domain controller

explanation: Endpoint DLP is not supported on Windows servers configured as domain controllers or installed with the Server Core option. Windows Server 2019 and later file servers, servers with Desktop Experience, and supported Azure Virtual Desktop hosts can all be onboarded and protected.

prompt: A company scopes an Endpoint DLP policy to a device group that contains all finance laptops and to a user group that contains only finance staff. A marketing employee signs in to one of the finance laptops and copies a protected file to a USB drive. What happens?

options.text: The policy is applied because the device is in scope
The policy is not applied because the user is not in scope
The policy is applied in audit-only mode because only one scope matches
The policy is applied and an alert is raised for the device owner

explanation: When a DLP policy that includes the Devices location is scoped by both users and devices, both the user and the device must be in scope for the policy to be enforced. Because the marketing employee is outside the user scope, the policy does not apply. DLP does not fall back to an audit-only mode or redirect alerts to a device owner when only one scope matches.

prompt: An administrator wants to pilot Endpoint DLP on six Windows 11 devices before a wider rollout. The devices are not managed by Intune, Configuration Manager or Group Policy. Which onboarding method is most appropriate?

options.text: The local script from the device onboarding page
The VDI onboarding script for non-persistent machines
The Microsoft Purview Information Protection scanner
A JAMF Pro configuration profile

explanation: The local onboarding script is intended for testing on a small number of machines (up to 10) and does not require a management platform. The VDI script is for non-persistent virtual desktops. The Information Protection scanner discovers and labels files in on-premises repositories and does not onboard devices. JAMF Pro is a macOS management tool, not a method for onboarding Windows devices.

prompt: A company wants Endpoint DLP to protect Mac computers used by its design team. Which statement about macOS support is correct?

options.text: Only the most recent macOS release is supported, and devices must be onboarded by using Group Policy
macOS devices are supported only if they also run the Microsoft Purview Information Protection client
The three latest released macOS versions are supported, and devices can be onboarded by using Intune or JAMF Pro
macOS devices are supported only for auditing; restrictive actions such as Block are not available

explanation: Endpoint DLP supports macOS devices running any of the three latest released versions, and Microsoft documents onboarding through Intune or JAMF Pro, with or without Defender for Endpoint. Group Policy does not manage macOS devices. The Information Protection client is a Windows labeling client and is not required. Activities such as copy to USB, print and upload can be restricted on macOS, not just audited.

prompt: An Endpoint DLP policy already restricts the clipboard, USB and print activities for all apps. The administrator adds Notepad to the Restricted apps list with the action Audit only for accessing protected items. A user opens a protected file in Notepad and tries to print it while the rule for all apps blocks Print. What happens?

options.text: The file cannot be opened because Notepad is a restricted app
The user can open and print the file because the restricted app setting takes priority
The user is prompted to override the block and must give a business justification
The user can open the file, and the print attempt is blocked

explanation: When the restricted app action is Audit only or Block with override, it controls only access to the file; after access is granted, the restrictions in File activities for all apps apply, so printing is blocked. The file would be inaccessible only if the restricted app action were Block. The restricted app setting does not take priority over other activity restrictions, and no override prompt appears because the print action is Block, not Block with override.

prompt: An app is listed on the Restricted apps list with the action Block and is also a member of a restricted app group that is added to the same DLP rule with Apply restrictions to a specific activity. Which settings does DLP apply when a user opens a protected file in the app?

options.text: The settings defined for the restricted app group
The settings defined on the Restricted apps list
The most restrictive setting from either configuration
The settings defined in File activities for all apps

explanation: Settings in a restricted app group override restrictions from the Restricted apps list and from File activities for all apps when they are in the same rule. DLP does not merge the configurations to choose the most restrictive one. File activities for all apps applies only to apps that are not governed by a restricted app group.

prompt: A company wants only a small set of approved applications to be able to open files that contain sensitive data on Windows devices; every other application must be blocked. The administrator wants to avoid maintaining a list of untrusted apps. What should the administrator configure?

options.text: Add every unapproved application executable to the Unallowed browsers list in Endpoint DLP settings
Create a restricted app group of approved apps set to Allow for all activity, and set access by apps not on the list to Block
Add the install folders of the approved applications to the File path exclusions for Windows list
Create a sensitive service domain group that contains the approved applications and set it to Allow

explanation: Microsoft documents an allow-list approach: put the approved apps in a restricted app group, apply the Allow restriction to all activity, and set access by apps that are not on the list to Block. The Unallowed browsers list only covers browsers and would still require listing untrusted apps. File path exclusions remove locations from DLP classification and protection entirely. Sensitive service domain groups contain websites, not applications.

prompt: An Endpoint DLP policy blocks copying engineering drawings to removable media. The IT team must still be able to copy them to two specific encrypted USB drives used for offsite backup. What should the administrator configure?

options.text: A file path exclusion for the drive letters of the backup drives
A printer group that contains the backup drives
A removable USB device group for the backup drives, set to Allow
An unallowed Bluetooth apps entry for the backup software

explanation: Removable USB device groups let an administrator assign different actions, such as Allow, to specific devices identified by properties such as serial number or vendor and product ID, while the global removable storage action stays Block. File path exclusions are based on paths, and drive letters change, so they would not identify the specific devices reliably. Printer groups define printers, and Bluetooth app lists control Bluetooth transfers.

prompt: A law firm wants an Endpoint DLP policy to block printing of contracts on all printers except those in the Legal department. What should the administrator create in the Endpoint DLP settings?

options.text: A printer group for the Legal printers, assigned the Allow action in the policy
A network share group that contains the Legal print server paths
A restricted app group that contains the print spooler
A VPN setting that limits printing to the corporate network

explanation: Printer groups let a policy apply actions to specific printers that differ from the global print action, so the Legal printers can be allowed while printing elsewhere is blocked. Network share groups apply to copying files to shares, not printing. Adding the spooler as a restricted app would not tell DLP which printers to permit. VPN settings control activities performed over a VPN connection and do not identify printers.

prompt: A company needs to block copying of CAD files that Endpoint DLP cannot scan to USB drives and network shares. Content inspection of these files is not required. Which approach should the administrator use?

options.text: Turn on optical character recognition so that DLP can read the CAD files
Use the Document could not be scanned condition with Apply restrictions to only unsupported file extensions
Add the CAD file extensions to the Disable classification setting in Endpoint DLP settings
Use the File extension is condition so that DLP scans the CAD files' contents

explanation: The Document could not be scanned condition combined with Apply restrictions to only unsupported file extensions restricts activities on file types that Endpoint DLP does not scan, without inspecting content. OCR adds image formats such as .jpg and .png, not CAD files. Disable classification stops scanning of listed extensions and does not add restrictions. File extension is triggers content scanning, which is unnecessary here and can use more device resources.

prompt: An Endpoint DLP rule blocks the Copy to clipboard activity for Word documents that contain sensitive data. A user copies a paragraph from a matching document and pastes it elsewhere in the same document. What happens?

options.text: The copy is blocked because the source content is sensitive
The copy is allowed only if the user enters a business justification
The paste is allowed because copying within the same file is permitted
The paste is allowed, but the document is moved to quarantine

explanation: For Block or Block with override on Copy to clipboard, copying and pasting within the same Office file is allowed; it is copying to other files or apps that is blocked. Business justification applies only to Block with override when the user crosses the restriction. Auto-quarantine is a restricted app feature for cloud sync apps, not a clipboard behaviour.

prompt: Users keep receiving repeated DLP notifications because the OneDrive sync app tries to upload files that a blocking DLP policy protects. The company wants these files moved to a secure folder with a text note left in their place. What should the administrator configure?

options.text: Add onedrive.exe to the Unallowed browsers list
Add the OneDrive folder to File path exclusions for Windows
Add onedrive.exe to a removable USB device group
Add onedrive.exe to the Restricted apps list with Auto-quarantine

explanation: Auto-quarantine on the Restricted apps list moves a sensitive item to an admin-configured folder when a restricted cloud sync app tries to access it, can leave a .txt placeholder, and stops the repeated notifications. The Unallowed browsers list applies to web browsers. Excluding the OneDrive folder would remove protection from the files. Removable USB device groups define storage hardware, not apps.

prompt: An investigation team wants a copy of every file that matches an Endpoint DLP rule on Windows devices so that they can review the actual content later. What must the administrator prepare before configuring this?

options.text: An Azure storage account and container with permissions configured
A Microsoft Purview Audit (Premium) license for each device
A SharePoint site with a Preservation Hold library
An eDiscovery (Premium) case with the devices added as data sources

explanation: Evidence collection for file activities on devices copies matched items to an Azure storage account, so the administrator must first create the storage account and container and configure permissions. Audit (Premium) licenses are assigned to users and do not store file copies. The Preservation Hold library is used by retention for SharePoint and OneDrive. eDiscovery cases do not collect files from Endpoint DLP matches.

prompt: A company wants users to be able to upload files that contain sensitive data only to its own partner portal domain; uploads of such files to any other website must be blocked. Users use Microsoft Edge. What should the administrator configure in Browser and domain restrictions?

options.text: Add the partner portal to the Unallowed browsers list
Set Service domains to Allow and add the partner portal domain
Add the partner portal to a VPN setting
Set Service domains to Block and add the partner portal domain

explanation: With Service domains set to Allow, uploads of protected files are permitted only to the listed domains and DLP enforces the policy action for every other domain. Setting Service domains to Block would do the opposite and restrict only the listed domain. The Unallowed browsers list holds browser executables, not websites, and VPN settings identify VPN connections.

prompt: A DLP policy blocks uploads of protected files to cloud services. The administrator adds a third-party browser to the Unallowed browsers list. A user tries to open a protected file in that browser. What does the user experience?

options.text: The file opens in the browser but is read-only
The file opens and any upload attempt is only audited
The browser is blocked and the user is told to open the file in Edge
The file is moved to the configured quarantine folder

explanation: Browsers on the Unallowed browsers list cannot access files that match an enforced policy with an upload restriction of Block or Block with override, and the user sees a toast notification telling them to open the file in Microsoft Edge. DLP does not open the file read-only or merely audit in this case. Quarantine is part of auto-quarantine for restricted apps, not of unallowed browsers.

prompt: When users override a Block with override action in Endpoint DLP, the compliance team wants them to pick a reason only from a fixed list, without typing free text. What should the administrator configure?

options.text: Set the business justification setting to Only show default options
Change the policy action from Block with override to Audit only
Turn off Always audit file activity for devices
Customize the user notification email for the policy

explanation: The global business justification setting in Endpoint DLP settings offers Only show default options, which restricts users to the built-in list of justifications. Changing the action to Audit only removes the override prompt entirely. Always audit file activity controls background auditing, and notification emails are separate from the justification choices in policy tips.

prompt: An administrator notices that Activity explorer shows file created and file modified events for Office and PDF files on onboarded devices that are not in any DLP policy. The organization wants to collect activity only for devices included in an active policy. What should the administrator do?

options.text: Offboard the devices and onboard them again
Turn off Always audit file activity for devices
Add the file types to Disable classification
Turn off Advanced classification scanning and protection

explanation: Always audit file activity for devices is on by default and audits activity for Office, PDF and CSV files even when no policy matches; turning it off limits auditing to devices in an active policy. Re-onboarding would not change the setting. Disable classification stops content scanning but does not stop activity auditing. Advanced classification controls cloud-based content scanning, not whether unmatched activities are audited.

prompt: An administrator wants to stop just-in-time protection from evaluating files in a build output folder on Windows devices, but the folder must still be covered by normal Endpoint DLP classification and policies. What should the administrator configure?

options.text: File path exclusions for Windows in Endpoint DLP settings
The Disable classification setting
File path exclusions in the just-in-time protection settings
A network share group for the folder

explanation: File path exclusions in the just-in-time protection settings exclude paths only from JIT evaluation, while Endpoint DLP still classifies and protects files there. File path exclusions for Windows in the general Endpoint DLP settings stop classification and protection for the path entirely. Disable classification works by file extension, not folder. A network share group applies actions to shares and does not exclude JIT evaluation.

prompt: A company is enabling just-in-time protection for Windows devices. During the pilot, management wants users to be able to complete their actions if file classification fails, rather than being blocked. Which setting should the administrator choose?

options.text: Turn on Control copying to clipboard in the just-in-time settings
Set Fallback action in case of failure to Allow users to complete actions
Set the policy action for all activities to Audit only
Add the users' main applications to the just-in-time app exclusions

explanation: The Fallback action in case of failure setting controls what happens when classification fails, and Allow users to complete actions lets the egress activity proceed. Control copying to clipboard adds more blocking while JIT evaluates. Changing every policy action to Audit only would weaken the policies themselves. App exclusions remove those applications from JIT evaluation altogether instead of setting the failure behaviour.

prompt: Before turning on just-in-time protection, an administrator must confirm that the Windows devices meet the prerequisites. Which component must be at the required minimum version?

options.text: The Microsoft Purview Information Protection client
The Microsoft Edge browser
The Microsoft Purview extension for Chrome
The Microsoft Defender antimalware client

explanation: Just-in-time protection requires antimalware client version 4.18.23080 or later, which can be checked with advanced hunting or the DLP diagnostics page. The Information Protection client, Edge version and the Chrome extension are not JIT prerequisites.

prompt: A security analyst needs to know which removable drive a user copied a sensitive file to, including the device manufacturer and serial number. Where can the analyst find this information?

options.text: The Copy to USB event details in Activity explorer
The Content explorer view for the sensitive information type
The Policy lookup page in Data lifecycle management
The device list on the Endpoint DLP onboarding page

explanation: Endpoint DLP records detailed attributes for audited activities, and Activity explorer shows them for a copy-to-USB event, including the removable media manufacturer, model and serial number. Content explorer shows where classified items are stored, not what was done with them. Policy lookup finds retention policies for users and sites. The device list shows onboarding and health status, not individual file activities.

prompt: A Windows laptop with Endpoint DLP policies is disconnected from the internet for a day. During that time the user tries to copy a previously classified sensitive file to USB, and the policy blocks it. When will the block event be visible in Activity explorer?

options.text: Immediately, because the event is recorded in the cloud service
Never, because offline enforcement events are discarded
After the device reconnects and the event is uploaded
Only after an administrator runs a new policy sync from the portal

explanation: Policies already pushed to an offline Windows device keep being enforced, but the enforcement events do not appear in Activity explorer until the device is back online. The event cannot reach the cloud while the device is offline, it is not discarded, and no manual sync by an administrator is needed.

prompt: In a single SharePoint site, contracts must be kept for 10 years, while meeting notes must be kept for 2 years. Both kinds of document are stored in the same library. What should the administrator use to meet the requirement?

options.text: One retention policy for the site with two retention periods
Two retention policies, each scoped to the same site
Retention labels, applied to the documents according to their type
A sensitivity label with a content expiry setting

explanation: Retention labels assign retention settings at the item level, so different documents in the same site can be kept for different periods. A retention policy applies one set of settings to every item in its locations, and two policies on the same site would combine by the principles of retention so every item would be kept for the longest period. Sensitivity labels control protection and access expiry, not retention and deletion.

prompt: An HR department must keep employee files for seven years after the employee leaves the company, not seven years after the files were created. Which configuration meets this requirement?

options.text: A retention policy that starts the retention period when items were last modified
A retention label configured for event-based retention
A retention policy that uses an adaptive scope based on the Department attribute
A retention label that starts the retention period when items were created

explanation: Event-based retention is available only with retention labels and starts the retention period when an event occurs, such as an employee leaving. Retention policies can start only from creation or last modified date, and an adaptive scope changes who is covered rather than when retention starts. A label based on creation date would start the clock too early.

prompt: Legal staff must review financial records before they are permanently deleted at the end of their retention period, and must be able to extend retention for selected items. What should the administrator configure?

options.text: A retention label with Start a disposition review as the action at the end of the retention period
A retention policy with the action Delete items automatically and an eDiscovery hold
A retention policy configured to retain items forever
An auto-apply sensitivity label policy for the financial records

explanation: Disposition review is available only with retention labels, and reviewers can approve disposal, relabel, extend or add reviewers. Retention policies do not support disposition review, and adding an eDiscovery hold or retaining forever would prevent deletion rather than enable a review. Sensitivity labels do not control end-of-retention actions.

prompt: A records manager is assigned as a disposition reviewer on a retention label but receives an access error when opening the Disposition page in the Microsoft Purview portal. The manager should not get other records management permissions. What should the administrator do?

options.text: Assign the manager the Global Administrator role in Microsoft Entra ID
Add the manager to the eDiscovery Manager role group
Add the manager as an owner of the mail-enabled security group used for disposition
Create a custom role group with the Disposition Management role and add the manager

explanation: Access to Disposition requires the Disposition Management role, and Microsoft recommends a custom role group with just that role when reviewers should not get other records management permissions. Global administrators are not granted Disposition Management by default. The eDiscovery Manager role group does not include it. For the mail-enabled security group used to show all disposition items, permissions go to members, not owners.

prompt: During a disposition review, a reviewer selects Extend for an item. What is the result?

options.text: The item is marked for permanent deletion, which happens within 15 days
Review is paused for the extended period, then restarts at the first stage
The item moves straight to the next configured stage of the disposition review
The item exits disposition and is governed by a different retention label

explanation: Extend suspends disposition review until the end of the extended period, after which the review is triggered again from the first stage. Approve disposal in the final stage marks the item for permanent deletion within 15 days, and in an interim stage moves it to the next stage. Relabel takes the item out of the review and applies another label's settings.

prompt: Mailboxes and OneDrive accounts of executives must have a longer retention period than those of other staff. Executives join and leave often, and the administrator does not want to update the policy each time. All executives have Executive as their job title in Microsoft Entra ID. What should the administrator configure?

options.text: A retention policy with a static scope that includes each executive's mailbox and OneDrive URL
A retention policy with a Users adaptive scope that queries the Job title attribute
A retention policy with a Microsoft 365 Groups adaptive scope for the executive team group
A retention label policy that publishes a label to all users

explanation: A Users adaptive scope runs a daily query against attributes such as Job title and applies to Exchange mailboxes and OneDrive accounts, so new executives are picked up automatically. A static scope must be edited whenever executives change, and OneDrive URLs change with UPNs. A Microsoft 365 Groups scope targets group mailboxes and sites, not individual users' mailboxes. A published label relies on users applying it.

prompt: An administrator needs a retention policy that applies only to modern communication sites and not to Microsoft 365 group-connected sites or OneDrive. Which configuration should be used?

options.text: A Microsoft 365 Groups adaptive scope that excludes group-connected sites
A Users adaptive scope with the advanced query IsInactiveMailbox -eq "False"
A static scope that includes all SharePoint classic and communication sites
A SharePoint sites adaptive scope with the KeyQL query SiteTemplate=SITEPAGEPUBLISHING

explanation: SharePoint site adaptive scopes use KeyQL in the advanced query builder, and SiteTemplate=SITEPAGEPUBLISHING selects only modern communication sites. A Microsoft 365 Groups scope targets groups, not site templates. The IsInactiveMailbox property applies to user scopes for mailboxes. The all-sites static option would include classic sites as well.

prompt: A compliance analyst must be allowed to create adaptive scopes for retention policies. Which role must be included in a role group that the analyst belongs to?

options.text: Scope Manager
Retention Management
Disposition Management
Data Classification Content Viewer

explanation: Any role group that has the Scope Manager role can create adaptive scopes; it is included in role groups such as Compliance Administrator and Records Management. Retention Management lets administrators manage retention policies and labels, Disposition Management covers disposition reviews, and Data Classification Content Viewer lets users view content in Content explorer; none of them grants the ability to create scopes.

prompt: An administrator creates a new adaptive scope for users in the Sales department and immediately adds it to a new retention policy. The next day, the scope details page shows only a few of the expected users. What is the most likely explanation?

options.text: Adaptive scopes support a maximum of 100 members
The policy must be in simulation mode before the scope is evaluated
Adaptive scopes cannot be used with Exchange mailboxes
Adaptive scope queries can take up to five days to fully populate

explanation: Adaptive scope queries run daily and can take up to five days to fully populate, so Microsoft recommends waiting a few days before adding a new scope to a policy. Adaptive scopes have no per-policy item limit and can cover very large memberships. Retention policies do not need simulation mode for scope evaluation, and Users scopes do apply to Exchange mailboxes.

prompt: Before using an advanced OPATH query in a Users adaptive scope, an administrator wants to confirm which mailboxes the query returns. What should the administrator do?

options.text: Run the query in SharePoint search at the tenant search page
Run Get-Recipient with the -Filter parameter in Exchange Online PowerShell
Use Policy lookup in Data lifecycle management
Run a content search in eDiscovery with the query as a keyword

explanation: Users and Microsoft 365 Groups scope queries use OPATH and can be validated with Get-Recipient, Get-Mailbox or Get-User and the -Filter parameter in Exchange Online PowerShell. SharePoint search validates KeyQL queries for site scopes. Policy lookup shows policies assigned to a user or site and does not test queries. An eDiscovery keyword search searches content, not recipient attributes.

prompt: An organization wants a retention policy that applies only to inactive mailboxes, to delete their content after three years. How can the administrator target only inactive mailboxes?

options.text: Use a static scope that includes the inactive mailboxes by name
Use a Microsoft 365 Groups adaptive scope with the Alias attribute
Use a Users adaptive scope with the advanced query builder and IsInactiveMailbox -eq "True"
Use a SharePoint sites adaptive scope that filters on RefinableString00

explanation: Targeting only inactive mailboxes requires a Users adaptive scope built with the advanced query builder and the OPATH property IsInactiveMailbox set to True. Static scopes do not support specifically including recipients with inactive mailboxes. Group and site scopes do not target user mailboxes.

prompt: A company must delete Microsoft Teams chat messages after one year. Which solution should the administrator use?

options.text: A retention label published to all users
An auto-apply retention label policy with a keyword query
A default retention label set on each team's document library
A retention policy for the Teams chats location

explanation: Teams messages do not support retention labels, so a retention policy that includes the Teams chats location must be used. Publishing or auto-applying a retention label covers Exchange, SharePoint, OneDrive and Microsoft 365 Groups content, not Teams messages. A default label on a document library affects files stored there, not chat messages.

prompt: Signed work visa documents must be retained for five years and must not be edited or deleted by users during that time. What should the administrator configure?

options.text: A retention label that marks items as a record
A retention policy that retains items for five years
A sensitivity label with Do Not Forward protection
A DLP policy that blocks sharing of the documents

explanation: A retention label that marks items as a record keeps the item and adds restrictions that block editing and deletion. A retention policy keeps copies of edited or deleted items in the Preservation Hold library but still lets users edit and delete the originals. Do Not Forward controls recipients' rights in email and does not stop deletion. A DLP policy controls sharing, not editing or deletion.

prompt: A site owner wants every document added to a specific SharePoint document library to get the Project - 5 Years retention label automatically. The label is already published to SharePoint. What should the site owner do?

options.text: Create an auto-apply retention label policy for the site
Set the label as the default retention label for the library
Apply a sensitivity label to the site that contains the library
Create a retention policy that is scoped to the library

explanation: A published retention label can be set as the default label for a SharePoint document library, folder or document set so that documents stored there inherit it. Creating an auto-apply policy needs compliance admin permissions and conditions such as sensitive info types or queries rather than a library location. Sensitivity labels on sites do not apply retention labels, and retention policies are scoped to sites, not individual libraries.

prompt: Any email or document in Exchange, SharePoint or OneDrive that contains a passport number must automatically receive a retention label that keeps it for six years. What should the administrator create?

options.text: A retention label policy that publishes the label to all locations
A retention policy with a sensitive information type condition
An auto-apply retention label policy that detects the passport number SIT
A DLP policy for all locations with the action Apply a retention label

explanation: Auto-apply retention label policies can apply a label to content that contains specific sensitive information types in Exchange, SharePoint, OneDrive and Microsoft 365 Groups. Publishing only makes the label available for manual use. Retention policies cannot use conditions such as sensitive info types. DLP policies can use retention labels as a condition but do not apply them.

prompt: A company wants to retain copies of files that users share as links in Outlook email and Teams messages, even if the original files are later changed or deleted. The administrator creates an auto-apply retention label policy for cloud attachments. What does Microsoft recommend for the label's retention start setting?

options.text: When items were labeled
When items were created
When items were last modified
When an event occurs

explanation: The cloud attachment copy in the Preservation Hold library is relabeled each time the unchanged file is shared again, so Microsoft recommends starting retention when items were labeled. Creation date is taken from the original file at the time of sharing, last modified has no effect for the copy, and event-based retention would require an event to be triggered.

prompt: An administrator creates an auto-apply retention label policy that applies the label Confidential - 7 Years to documents that contain bank account numbers. Some of the matching documents already have a standard retention label that a user applied manually. What happens to those documents?

options.text: The auto-applied label replaces the manually applied label
Both labels are applied, and the longer retention period wins
The documents are moved to disposition review
The existing manually applied label stays on the documents

explanation: An item can have only one retention label at a time, and an auto-apply retention label policy does not replace or remove an existing retention label. Retention labels cannot be stacked on one item. Disposition review happens only at the end of a retention period for labels configured with that action.

prompt: A document in a SharePoint site is subject to a retention policy that retains all site content for seven years and then deletes it. A user applies a retention label to the document that retains it for five years and then deletes it. What is the outcome?

options.text: The document is deleted after five years because the label's delete action takes precedence
The document is retained for seven years and then deleted
The document is retained indefinitely because two retention settings conflict
The document is deleted after five years because the shortest period wins

explanation: Retention takes precedence over deletion and the longest retention period wins, so the document is kept for seven years; the label's delete action then applies at the end of that period. The label's delete action has precedence over the policy's delete action but cannot remove the document while another setting still retains it. Conflicting settings do not cause indefinite retention. Shortest deletion wins applies only when the earlier principles do not decide the outcome.

prompt: A retention policy deletes all email after 10 years and does not retain it. A delete-only retention label that deletes items after one year is applied to project emails. When are the project emails permanently deleted?

options.text: After 10 years, because the policy covers the whole mailbox and all its folders
After 10 years, because the longest period always wins in a conflict
Never, until an administrator releases the retention policy for the mailbox
After one year, because a label's delete action wins over a policy's

explanation: Neither setting retains the email, so only deletion conflicts remain; a retention label provides explicit settings and its delete action takes precedence over a retention policy's delete action, so the emails are deleted after one year. Longest retention wins applies only to retain actions. The policy's broader coverage does not override the label, and no release is needed.

prompt: Two retention policies apply to a user's mailbox and neither retains content. An org-wide policy for all mailboxes deletes items after 10 years. A second policy that includes this specific user deletes items after five years. When are the user's items deleted?

options.text: After five years, because the policy that names the user wins
After 10 years, because the org-wide policy was created first
After 10 years, because the longest period always wins
After seven and a half years, as an average of both deletion settings

explanation: When only retention policies apply, a policy with an adaptive scope or a static scope that includes specific instances takes precedence over an org-wide static scope for deletion, so items are deleted after five years. The order in which policies were created does not matter. Longest period wins applies to retain actions, not delete-only settings, and retention settings are never averaged.

prompt: An administrator needs to list all retention policies and retention label policies that currently apply to a particular SharePoint site. What should the administrator use?

options.text: Content explorer, filtered by the retention labels used on the site
Activity explorer, filtered by the site URL and retention activities
Policy lookup in Data lifecycle management
The Adaptive scopes page, using Scope details

explanation: Policy lookup in Data lifecycle management or Records management finds the policies for retention assigned to a specific user, site or Microsoft 365 group, and requires the exact URL or email address without wildcards. Content explorer and Activity explorer show labeled items and activities, not assigned policies. Scope details list the members of an adaptive scope, not the static policies that apply to a site.

prompt: A SharePoint site is covered by a retention policy that retains content for five years. A user deletes a file and then empties the site recycle bins. Three months later, legal counsel needs the file. How should the administrator recover it?

options.text: Restore it from the user's OneDrive recycle bin
Use an eDiscovery search to find the copy in the site's Preservation Hold library and export it
Restore the site from a SharePoint backup
Ask Microsoft Support to recover the file from the Recoverable Items folder

explanation: When a file under a retention policy is deleted, a copy is kept in the site's hidden Preservation Hold library, and Microsoft directs administrators to use compliance tools such as eDiscovery to access these retained files. The OneDrive recycle bin does not hold SharePoint site files. Restoring from a backup is unnecessary, and the Recoverable Items folder belongs to Exchange mailboxes, not SharePoint sites.

prompt: A retention policy retains SharePoint files for three years and then deletes them. A file that was never modified reaches the end of its retention period and is removed. Where can a site collection administrator restore it, and for how long?

options.text: From the first-stage or second-stage Recycle Bin, within 93 days
From the Preservation Hold library, for 30 days
From the Recoverable Items folder, for 14 days
It cannot be restored because deletion by a retention policy is immediate

explanation: Unmodified content is moved to the first-stage Recycle Bin at the end of the retention period, and a 93-day period spans both recycle bin stages before permanent deletion; site collection administrators can restore from either stage. Unmodified files are not copied to the Preservation Hold library. The Recoverable Items folder is part of Exchange. Deletion by retention settings is not immediate.

prompt: A regulator requires that a retention policy for financial records cannot be turned off, deleted or made less restrictive, even by administrators. The policy currently uses an adaptive scope. What must the administrator do?

options.text: Apply Preservation Lock to the existing adaptive policy
Convert the policy to a retention label policy
Mark the records as regulatory records by using a DLP policy
Use a static scope for the policy and then apply Preservation Lock

explanation: Preservation Lock restricts changes so a policy cannot be turned off, deleted or made less restrictive, but adaptive scopes do not support Preservation Lock, so the policy must use a static scope. Converting to a label policy does not by itself lock it. DLP policies do not mark content as regulatory records.

prompt: An administrator must create a retention policy that covers Exchange public folders. Which scope option must be used?

options.text: A Users adaptive scope
A Microsoft 365 Groups adaptive scope
A static scope
A SharePoint sites adaptive scope

explanation: The Exchange public folders and Skype for Business locations do not support adaptive scopes, so the policy must use a static scope. Users, Microsoft 365 Groups and SharePoint sites adaptive scopes apply to other locations such as mailboxes, group content and sites.

prompt: An investigator must be able to review alerts and cases in Insider Risk Management, including the files copied into a case's Content explorer and forensic evidence clips. The investigator must not be able to change policies or settings. Which role group should the investigator be added to?

options.text: Insider Risk Management Analysts
Insider Risk Management Admins
Insider Risk Management Investigators
Insider Risk Management Auditors

explanation: Insider Risk Management Investigators can access alerts and cases, view forensic evidence captures and view case content in Content explorer, but cannot configure policies or settings. Analysts can work with alerts and cases but cannot view forensic evidence or Content explorer. Admins configure policies and settings but cannot investigate alerts. Auditors can only view and export the Insider Risk Management audit logs.

prompt: A company requires that forensic evidence capturing for a user be approved by a member of the HR team. HR staff must not be able to view alerts, cases or captured clips. Which role group should the HR approvers be added to?

options.text: Insider Risk Management Approvers
Insider Risk Management Investigators
Insider Risk Management
Insider Risk Management Admins

explanation: The Insider Risk Management Approvers role group can approve forensic evidence capturing requests without access to alerts, cases or captures. Investigators can view captures but cannot approve requests. The full Insider Risk Management role group grants every permission, including viewing alerts and evidence. Admins can create capturing requests but cannot approve them.

prompt: An internal audit team must be able to view and export the audit log of actions taken in Insider Risk Management, without any access to alerts, cases or policy configuration. Which role group meets this requirement?

options.text: Insider Risk Management Analysts
Insider Risk Management Auditors
Insider Risk Management Admins
Insider Risk Management Approvers

explanation: Insider Risk Management Auditors can view and export Insider Risk Management audit logs and have no access to alerts, cases or configuration. Analysts investigate alerts and cases, Admins configure policies and settings, and Approvers approve forensic evidence requests; none of them is limited to audit log access.

prompt: An organization wants to detect data theft by employees who have resigned. Resignation and last working dates are kept in a third-party HR system that can export CSV files. What should the administrator configure so that the policy can use these dates?

options.text: The Physical badging connector
The Insider Risk Indicators connector
A Microsoft Healthcare connector
The Microsoft 365 HR connector

explanation: The Microsoft 365 HR connector imports HR data from CSV files, including termination and last employment dates, and is required by templates such as departing user data theft. The Physical badging connector imports building access events in JSON format. The Insider Risk Indicators connector imports preprocessed detections from SIEM solutions. The Healthcare connector imports EMR activity for patient data misuse.

prompt: A hospital wants Insider Risk Management to detect staff who access patient records improperly in its electronic medical record (EMR) system. Which policy template and connector should the administrator use?

options.text: Data leaks with the Insider Risk Indicators connector
Security policy violations with Microsoft Defender for Endpoint
Patient data misuse with a Microsoft Healthcare connector
Risky browser usage with the Physical badging connector

explanation: The Patient data misuse template requires a Microsoft Healthcare connector, which imports EMR activity such as improper patient record access, and it also requires the HR connector. Data leaks focuses on exfiltration of sensitive content. Security policy violations uses Defender for Endpoint alerts. Risky browser usage detects browsing behaviour, and badging data does not reveal record access in an EMR system.

prompt: A company configures the Physical badging connector so that insider risk policies can detect unusual building access by employees who are about to leave. Testing shows only unauthorized physical access events are processed, with no correlation to departing users. What is missing?

options.text: The Microsoft 365 HR connector
Microsoft Defender for Endpoint integration
A priority user group
The Microsoft Purview browser extension

explanation: To correlate badging events with departing and terminated users, the Microsoft 365 HR connector must also be configured; without it, policies process only unauthorized physical access events. Defender for Endpoint provides security violation alerts, priority user groups target sensitive roles, and the browser extension supports browsing indicators; none of these supplies departure dates.

prompt: A security team uses Splunk to aggregate risky activity detections from Salesforce and wants to use them as triggers and indicators in Insider Risk Management policies. What should the administrator configure?

options.text: A Microsoft 365 HR connector that imports the Splunk CSV export
The Insider Risk Indicators connector with a sample file of the aggregated detections
A cloud app connector in Microsoft Defender for Cloud Apps for Splunk
An Audit (Premium) retention policy for Salesforce events

explanation: The Insider Risk Indicators connector imports preprocessed, aggregated detections from SIEM solutions such as Microsoft Sentinel or Splunk, and its workflow uses a sample file to configure the schema; the custom indicators can then be triggers or policy indicators. The HR connector imports HR data such as termination dates. Defender for Cloud Apps connectors provide cloud storage and service indicators for apps like Box or Amazon S3, not Splunk output. Audit retention policies do not create IRM indicators.

prompt: An administrator creates a policy from the Security policy violations template, but no alerts are generated even though Microsoft Defender for Endpoint raises alerts for the users' devices. What should the administrator do?

options.text: Configure the Microsoft 365 HR connector and add it to the policy
Turn on device monitoring for Endpoint DLP in the Purview portal
Assign Microsoft Purview Audit (Premium) to the users
Share endpoint alerts with Purview in Defender for Endpoint settings

explanation: Security policy violation templates use Defender for Endpoint alerts, which are imported only after the Insider Risk Management integration is enabled in the Defender for Endpoint advanced features. The HR connector is needed only for departing or risky user variants of the template. Endpoint DLP device monitoring provides device activity indicators, not Defender security alerts. Audit (Premium) does not import Defender alerts.

prompt: Insider risk analysts see pseudonymized user names such as AnonIS8-988 in alerts. The legal department approves showing actual user names to analysts. Where should the administrator change this?

options.text: In the Privacy section of Insider Risk Management settings
In the Policy indicators section of Insider Risk Management settings
In the user's Microsoft Entra ID profile
In the Data loss prevention settings for user notifications

explanation: The Privacy setting in Insider Risk Management settings controls whether anonymized versions of user names are shown. Policy indicators control which activities are detected. Entra ID profile settings do not affect pseudonymization in Insider Risk Management, and DLP notification settings apply to DLP policy tips.

prompt: While creating an Insider Risk Management policy, an administrator finds that the device indicators on the Policy indicators page are greyed out and cannot be selected. What should the administrator do?

options.text: Assign the administrator to the Insider Risk Management Analysts role group
Create a priority user group for the users in scope
Change the policy scope to include all users and groups
Turn on the indicators in Insider Risk Management settings on the Policy indicators page

explanation: Indicators must be turned on globally in Insider Risk Management settings (Policy indicators) before they can be selected in a policy; the policy wizard offers a Turn on indicators prompt that leads there. Analysts cannot configure policies, so that role would not help. Priority user groups and the all-users scope do not enable indicators.

prompt: A company wants to score risky activities more strictly for users in finance leadership roles who have broad access to confidential data. Which policy template should the administrator choose?

options.text: Data theft by departing users
Data leaks by priority users
Risky browser usage
Patient data misuse

explanation: Data leaks by priority users targets leaks by users in a priority user group, such as people in critical positions with high levels of data access; a priority user group is required for this template. The departing users template focuses on users who are leaving. Risky browser usage detects browsing to potentially inappropriate sites. Patient data misuse targets EMR systems.

prompt: An administrator wants an Insider Risk Management policy based on the Data leaks template to start scoring users when they match an existing DLP policy. Users match the DLP policy, but no insider risk alerts appear. What should the administrator check in the DLP policy?

options.text: That the policy is in simulation mode
That the policy includes the Devices location
That user notifications are turned off
That the Incident reports setting uses High severity

explanation: Insider Risk Management alerts are not generated from DLP policies whose Incident reports severity is Low or Medium, so the DLP rule must report at High severity. Simulation mode would prevent enforcement rather than help. The Devices location is not required for the trigger. User notifications do not affect whether insider risk scoring starts.

prompt: A compliance team wants to evaluate potential insider risks across the tenant to decide which policies to create, before configuring any Insider Risk Management policies. What should the administrator do?

options.text: Create a policy from each template in test mode
Export the audit log and analyze it in Excel
Run an analytics scan from the Insider Risk Management overview
Create a forensic evidence policy that captures all activities

explanation: Insider risk analytics scans user activity without any policies configured and provides insight reports, which can take up to 48 hours, to help determine which policies to create. Creating policies from every template is unnecessary and generates alerts. Manual audit log analysis does not apply the insider risk models. Forensic evidence requires approved users and is not a discovery tool.

prompt: An administrator turns on forensic evidence capturing and creates a forensic evidence policy. Captures are not recorded from a target user's Windows 11 device. The device is onboarded to Microsoft Purview, and the user's capture request was approved. What else is required?

options.text: The Microsoft Purview Information Protection client must be installed
The Microsoft Purview Client must be installed on the device
The device must be enrolled in Windows Autopilot
Endpoint DLP just-in-time protection must be enabled

explanation: To capture forensic evidence, devices must be onboarded to the Microsoft Purview portal and have the Microsoft Purview Client installed, which can be downloaded from the forensic evidence Client installation page. The Information Protection client is for labeling files. Autopilot is a provisioning service and is not required. Just-in-time protection is an Endpoint DLP feature unrelated to visual capture.

prompt: An organization wants forensic evidence to record clips only when approved users print files or copy them to USB, to reduce storage and protect privacy. How should the forensic evidence policy be configured?

options.text: With the All activities scope, excluding every app except the print spooler
With the All activities scope and a 10-second capturing window
With the Specific activities scope and only the printing and USB device activities selected
With the Specific activities scope and every device indicator selected

explanation: A forensic evidence policy with the Specific activities scope captures only the device activities selected, such as printing or copying to USB. The All activities scope captures everything approved users do, and exclusions only remove listed apps and websites. Selecting every device indicator would capture far more than the two required activities, and the capturing window only sets clip length.

prompt: A user is approved for two forensic evidence policies: one that captures all activities and one that captures only specific activities. Which statement describes the capturing behaviour?

options.text: The specific activities policy takes precedence because it is more restrictive
Neither policy captures until one of them is removed
Clips are captured only during the activation window of the newest policy
The continuous (all activities) policy takes precedence

explanation: Continuous forensic evidence policies that capture all activities take precedence over selective policies that capture only specific activities. The more restrictive policy does not win, policies do not block each other, and capture is not tied to the newest policy's activation window.

prompt: A company with no existing insider risk or DLP policies wants to start using Adaptive Protection as quickly as possible. It uses the quick setup option. Which statement describes what quick setup creates?

options.text: An insider risk policy from the Data leaks template, and two DLP policies that start in test mode
An insider risk policy from the Security policy violations template, and DLP policies that block immediately
Only the insider risk levels; the DLP policies must be created manually
An insider risk policy, and Conditional Access policies that block elevated-risk users immediately

explanation: Quick setup creates an insider risk policy based on the Data leaks template and two DLP policies, one for Endpoint DLP and one for Teams and Exchange, that start in test (audit-only) mode. It does not use the Security policy violations template or block immediately. It creates DLP policies for you, and the Conditional Access policy it creates is in report-only mode so users are not blocked.

prompt: An administrator edits an existing DLP policy so that users assigned the Elevated insider risk level are blocked from sharing sensitive files. Which condition must the DLP rule include, and which locations does Adaptive Protection support?

options.text: Content is shared from Microsoft 365, for SharePoint and OneDrive only
User's insider risk level for Adaptive Protection is, for Exchange, Teams and devices
Sender is a member of the priority user group, for Exchange only
Document property is, for all DLP locations

explanation: A DLP policy for Adaptive Protection must include the condition User's insider risk level for Adaptive Protection is, and Adaptive Protection currently supports the Exchange, Teams and Devices locations. The Content is shared condition does not use risk levels, and SharePoint and OneDrive are not supported for Adaptive Protection. Priority user groups are Insider Risk Management settings, not DLP conditions, and document properties do not reflect user risk.

prompt: In Adaptive Protection, users keep their Elevated insider risk level for seven days and then it resets. The security team wants the level to last 14 days. Which setting should the administrator change?

options.text: Past activity detection
Policy timeframes in Insider Risk Management settings
Insider risk level timeframe
Alert volume in Intelligent detections

explanation: The Insider risk level timeframe setting controls how long an insider risk level stays assigned before it resets automatically; the default is 7 days and it can be set from 5 to 30 days. Past activity detection sets how many days back Adaptive Protection looks for activity that meets the level conditions. Policy timeframes control the activation window for policies, and Alert volume controls how many alerts are generated.

prompt: After an investigation, an analyst determines that a user was wrongly assigned the Elevated risk level in Adaptive Protection. The analyst wants to remove the level now without changing the policy. What should the analyst do?

options.text: Turn off Adaptive Protection for the tenant
Delete the user's insider risk alerts from the Alerts dashboard
Remove the user from the DLP policy scope
Select the user on the assigned risk levels tab and choose Expire

explanation: Selecting a user on the Users assigned insider risk levels tab and choosing Expire manually resets that user's insider risk level without removing existing alerts or cases. Turning off Adaptive Protection resets every user's level and stops the feature for the whole tenant. Alerts are dismissed rather than deleted, and removing the user from the DLP policy changes the policy instead of the risk level.

prompt: A security team wants to block users with the Elevated insider risk level from signing in to Office 365 apps. The Insider Risk Management administrator has already turned on Adaptive Protection. Who must create the blocking policy, and where?

options.text: A Conditional Access Administrator, in the Microsoft Entra admin center
An Insider Risk Management Admin, in the Insider Risk Management policies page
A DLP Compliance Management member, in a DLP policy for the Office 365 apps
An Exchange administrator, by using an Exchange Online mail flow rule

explanation: Blocking app access is done with a Conditional Access policy that uses the Insider risk condition, created in the Microsoft Entra admin center by a Global Administrator, Conditional Access Administrator or Security Administrator. Insider Risk Management Admins configure insider risk policies and Adaptive Protection but not Conditional Access. DLP policies restrict content actions, not sign-in. Mail flow rules affect email only.

prompt: An analyst reviews an insider risk alert and decides it needs a deeper investigation with notes, content review and possible legal action. What should the analyst do with the alert?

options.text: Dismiss the alert and open an eDiscovery (Standard) case
Resolve the alert as Benign
Confirm the alert and create an insider risk case
Assign the alert to the Insider Risk Management Auditors role group

explanation: Confirming an alert creates an insider risk case, where analysts and investigators can add notes, review user activity and content, and take actions such as escalating for investigation. Dismissing the alert would close it as not needing action, and Resolving as Benign is a case outcome for low-risk results. Auditors can only view audit logs and cannot investigate alerts.

prompt: An investigator decides that a user's risky activity was accidental and wants to send the user a reminder about the data handling policy, while keeping the case open to watch for further activity. What should the investigator do?

options.text: Resolve the case as Benign, which automatically emails the user
Use Send email notice with a notice template from the case
Escalate the case for investigation
Add a case note addressed to the user

explanation: Send email notice sends a message to the user generated from a notice template, and sending a notice does not close the case. Resolving the case closes it and does not send a notice automatically. Escalating creates an eDiscovery (Premium) case for legal review. Case notes are visible only to reviewers of the case, not sent to the user.

prompt: An insider risk case requires legal review, preservation of the user's content and a legal hold notification workflow. Which case action should the investigator use?

options.text: Escalate for investigation
Run a Power Automate flow to notify the user's manager
Resolve the case as Confirmed policy violation
Create a Microsoft Teams team for the case

explanation: Escalate for investigation creates a new eDiscovery (Premium) case, which provides preservation, collection, review and legal hold notification workflows. A Power Automate flow can notify a manager but does not preserve content. Resolving the case closes it. A Teams team supports collaboration but provides no legal hold workflow.

prompt: After reviewing a case, an investigator finds that the alerts were false positives caused by a planned data migration. How should the investigator close the case?

options.text: Resolve the case as Confirmed policy violation
Send an email notice and leave the case active
Resolve the case as Benign
Escalate the case to eDiscovery (Premium) and close it there

explanation: Benign is the resolution classification for cases whose alerts are low risk, not serious or false positives, and resolving changes the case status to Closed. Confirmed policy violation is for risky or malicious activity. Sending a notice leaves the case open. Escalating to eDiscovery is for legal investigation, not closing false positives.

prompt: A company buys Microsoft 365 E5 licenses for its finance users so that Audit (Premium) events are logged for them. After the licenses are assigned, Audit (Premium) events still do not appear for some users. What should the administrator check in the Microsoft 365 admin center?

options.text: That the Microsoft 365 Advanced Auditing app is selected under each user's licenses and apps
That each user is a member of the Audit Manager role group
That mailbox auditing is turned off for each user so that Premium auditing can take over
That an audit log retention policy exists for each user

explanation: Audit (Premium) requires an appropriate E5 or add-on license and the Microsoft 365 Advanced Auditing app or service plan enabled for the user; logging of Premium insights begins within 24 hours. The Audit Manager role group gives permission to search the log and manage audit settings, not to generate Premium events. Mailbox auditing must stay on. Retention policies control how long records are kept, not whether they are logged.
